sens: Report a news, convey information to someone
Make known publicly an event
Communicate a received word
G6000.detail:
1. To announce is to transmit information, to report news to someone who does not yet know it. It is the verb of the messenger, the one who brings fresh news. In John 20:18, Mary Magdalene "announces" to the disciples that she has seen the risen Jesus: she reports to them what she has just experienced, what she has seen and heard from His own mouth.
2. The word also emphasizes the idea of making important information known publicly or solemnly. It is not mere chatter: it is to carry news worthy of being heard, intended to be received and retained.
3. To announce can also mean to communicate, to transmit a word, a message received from elsewhere. Mary announces not only what she has seen, but also "what He had told her": she is a bearer of a word from the Lord.
G6000.origine: The verb ἀγγέλλω comes from the family of the word ἄγγελος (angelos), which means "messenger," "angel." It is the verb of the messenger: the one who carries news, who "makes known" (angellō = to make known). In classical Greek, it expresses the action of reporting, revealing, carrying information. The root reflects the idea of transmitting, communicating something important.
G6000.emploi: This verb appears only once in John 20:18, in the ultimate context of the Resurrection. It is Mary Magdalene who uses it when announcing to the disciples her encounter with the risen Christ. The context is solemn: it is the moment when the Resurrection, the central event of Christian salvation, begins to be transmitted from eyewitnesses to the group of disciples. The verb "announce" emphasizes the act of communication, the transmission of a living and central news for the faith.
G6000.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is transmitted through the living word of those who have encountered Christ. Mary does not keep the experience to herself: she announces it, she shares it. For the reader, this shows that every Christian can be a bearer of the good news, a messenger in turn. The announcement of the Resurrection is never silent; it demands to be spoken, to be shared from ear to ear, from heart to heart.

sens: Container or receptacle used to store or transport objects
Receptacle intended to receive or collect something
G6001.detail:
1. A vase is a container, typically made of ceramic or glass, used to hold and preserve things. In the parable of the net in Matthew 13:48, after the miraculous catch, the fishermen put "the good into vessels, but threw the bad away" — the vase here is a simple practical container for sorting and storing fresh fish.
2. By extension, the word designates any receptacle used to collect or transport something, not just for cooking or storage. It is a neutral and general term for any hollow object designed to contain.
G6001.origine: The Greek word ἄγγος comes from a root expressing the idea of "to contain" or "to receive." In Hebrew and Aramaic, it translates the words כְּלִי (keli, "utensil") and כְּלוּב (keluv, "cage" or "container"). This term belongs to the ordinary vocabulary of homes and trades, without any particular connotation — it is simply the word to designate an object that receives or carries other things.
G6001.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 13:48, at the heart of the parable of the net. Jesus describes the fishermen who, after filling their net with fish of all kinds, sort them by placing the good fish into vessels: the good fish goes into the vessels, the bad is rejected. This context shows that the vase is a practical and common utensil used for organization and preservation during daily work. The image evokes order and sorting, not the object itself.
G6001.portee: This parable reminds us that God, at the end of time, will separate the righteous from the wicked — an inevitable and definitive sorting. The vase, though ordinary, participates in Jesus' teaching on divine judgment: it represents the order that God imposes, the distinction between what deserves to be preserved and what must be rejected. For the Christian, it is an invitation to seriously consider one's own fate on the day of judgment.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke
G6002.detail: Admin is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, as a link in a genealogical chain. In Luke 3:33, he appears in the genealogy of Jesus presented by Luke: Admin is the son of Aminadab and the father of Arni. This genealogy traces back to Judah, one of the twelve sons of Jacob, which shows that Jesus was from the royal and holy lineage of God's people.
G6002.origine: Admin is a Hebrew or Aramaic name. It appears in the Hebrew Old Testament in a similar form (it is sometimes associated with Admatha or Admatha). In Luke's genealogy, this name is part of a long succession of ancestors that establishes the historical and theological continuity between Judah and Jesus.
G6002.emploi: Admin appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:33. Luke places this man in his genealogy of Jesus, which traces back to David and Judah. This genealogy, different from the one given by Matthew, affirms that Jesus is a true descendant of Israel and heir to the promises made to God's people. Admin is one link among many others, most of whom are unknown elsewhere in the Bible.
G6002.portee: Admin reminds us that Jesus did not fall from the sky: He is rooted in the real history of Israel, with concrete ancestors, obscure or famous. His existence in this genealogy affirms the authentic incarnation of the Son of God and God's faithfulness to His promises to His people.

sens: Gather together a group of people
Collect in a crowd
Converge to the same place
G6003.detail:
1. To assemble means to gather together a group of people for a common purpose. It is to bring together those who were scattered. In Luke 24:33, the disciples returning from the road to Emmaus find the eleven apostles and other believers assembled in one place in Jerusalem to meet.
2. The word also suggests the idea of gathering in a crowd or compact group. The image is of people coming closer together to form a whole.
3. To assemble can also refer to the movement by which different people converge to the same place, as when gathering for an event or special occasion.
G6003.origine: The word comes from a root that designates noise or tumult (θρόος) and evokes the idea of a noisy and agitated crowd gathering. The adjective ἀθρόος means "gathered in a crowd." It is a verb that expresses the action of gathering into a compact group, often with the dynamic image of people converging together.
G6003.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 24:33. It is just after the two disciples from Emmaus have recognized the risen Lord and return to Jerusalem. They find the eleven apostles and other believers assembled together — a gathering that expresses the unity and cohesion of the apostolic community at the very moment of the resurrection.
G6003.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of assembly and communion among believers. The church is defined as a people gathered around the risen Lord. This gathering of the disciples expresses the life of the early church: people coming together to share faith, encourage one another, and live together the reality of the resurrection.

sens: To dress someone or cover something with clothing or a protective layer
To provide, adorn, or embellish (in a figurative sense)
G6005.detail:
1. To clothe means primarily to put clothes on someone, to cover them with garments. This is the concrete, physical sense: God clothes the grass of the fields with beautiful appearance (Luke 12:28). The image evokes a garment that envelops and protects.
2. The word takes on a broader and figurative meaning: to clothe can mean to provide someone with something, to give or present it to them. Jesus uses it in this way to say that God "clothes" creatures with what they need, endowing them, adorning them with beauty and grace.
G6005.origine: The Greek word ἀμφιάζω comes from the root ἀμφί ("on both sides," "all around"), which expresses the idea of enveloping or covering from all sides. It is a Hellenistic form (the Greek spoken after Alexander) of the verb ἀμφιέννυμι, which has the same meaning. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this verb translates the Hebrew word לָבַשׁ (labash), "to clothe," which carries the same image: to cover the entire body.
G6005.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Gospels, in Luke 12:28, in a teaching of Jesus about trusting God. Jesus uses this word to speak of how God "clothes" the grass of the fields with a magnificent adornment, even though it lasts only a day. It is an argument "a fortiori": if God takes care to clothe ephemeral plants, He will certainly take care to clothe His children. The context is one of exhortation not to worry about food and clothing.
G6005.portee: This word invites the Christian to meditate on divine providence. By contemplating how God generously and beautifully clothes nature, even for what is temporary, we learn to trust Him for our daily needs. It is an invitation to free our hearts from material anxiety and to recognize that our Heavenly Father watches over us with infinitely more care.

sens: To throw a fishing net into the water
To surround or cover something by throwing over it
G6006.detail:
1. To throw a fishing net into the water to catch fish. This is the sense seen in Mark 1:16, where Simon and Andrew "were casting" a net into the Sea of Galilee as professional fishermen. The word designates this specific gesture of the fisherman who casts his net in an arc to deploy it on the surface of the water.
2. More broadly, the verb means "to throw around" or "to surround by throwing" — hence its connection with the word "clothing." The image is of something projected around someone or something to cover or capture it.
G6006.origine: The Greek word comes from two prefixes: "amphi" (around, on both sides) and "ballō" (to throw, to cast). It thus evokes the idea of throwing something around, surrounding it with a circular motion. It is a verb formed to express a very concrete and material action: the gesture of the fisherman who spreads his net in a circle around the fish.
G6006.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament in Mark 1:16. It designates the characteristic action of the Galilean fisherman casting his fishing net. Although the word is rare in the New Testament, it is very expressive in this context: Jesus calls Simon and Andrew at the moment they are engaged in their trade, just before inviting them to become "fishers of men." The context thus shows the transition from earthly work (casting the net for fish) to spiritual vocation.
G6006.portee: This word helps us to concretely imagine the moment when Jesus recruits His first disciples by the lake. It reminds us that Jesus calls ordinary people, engaged in their daily work, and invites them to enter into a new mission. The contrast between the net cast in the sea and the future mission of "fishers of men" shows how Jesus transforms an ordinary profession into a symbol of a spiritual mission.

sens: A fragrant plant or substance of Indian origin used as a spice or perfume
In the context of trade, a prized and costly luxury good
G6007.detail:
1. An aromatic substance is a plant or a preparation made from a plant originating from India, emitting a pleasant fragrance. It was used as a spice in cooking or as a base for perfume — a rare and precious product, reserved for the elite. In Revelation 18:13, the aromatic substance is among the luxurious goods that merchants bought in Babylon: cinnamon, perfumes, myrrh, incense — all costly substances imported from afar.
2. The word also designates, more broadly in this apocalyptic context, the lucrative trade of rare and fragrant goods, symbolizing the wealth and opulent commerce of the great city. These aromatics represent the splendor of the world, the pursuit of pleasures and temporal riches that will be lost during the fall of Babylon.
G6007.origine: The Greek word amōmon likely comes from a South Asian language, as the product itself originated there. It designates an Indian plant belonging to the ginger family, close to cardamom or amomum. The term was borrowed by Greek and then by Latin (amomum), and appears in lists of spices and perfumes from the ancient world. It is a specialized word from the international trade of the first century.
G6007.emploi: The aromatic substance appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:13, in the apocalyptic description of the fall of Great Babylon. John enumerates the luxury goods that merchants from around the world sold to the city: gold, silver, precious stones, pearls, fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet, fragrant wood, ivory — and among them, the aromatics. This entire list symbolizes earthly wealth, commercial pride, and attachment to perishable goods that God's judgment will sweep away.
G6007.portee: For the Christian reader, the aromatic substance evokes the vanity of earthly riches and worldly commerce. Like all the luxuries listed in Revelation 18, it reminds us that the pursuit of pleasures and costly goods is vain — all will be destroyed at judgment. This word invites the believer not to set their heart on perishable things, no matter how beautiful or precious they may be, but on the eternal realities of the Kingdom of God.

sens: To rise suddenly and vigorously
To spring, to jump with energy
To rush towards someone
G6008.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of standing up or getting up with a quick and energetic gesture, often after having been sitting or lying down. It is a sudden impulse of the body. In Mark 10:50, blind Bartimaeus, sitting by the roadside, leaps up upon hearing Jesus.
2. The word evokes less a simple gesture than a movement of jumping or leaping, something dynamic and impatient. The prefix "ana-" (upward) reinforces this idea of an upward and vigorous movement.
3. In the context of Mark 10:50, this leap also expresses eagerness and urgency: Bartimaeus cannot wait; he leaps to get closer to Jesus as soon as he hears Him call.
G6008.origine: The verb is composed of the prefix "ana-" (upward, again) and the verb "pēdaō" which means to jump or leap. The latter evokes the image of an animal leap or an athletic gesture. The root "pēd-" belongs to the family of lively and energetic movements, close to the idea of momentum.
G6008.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 10:50. It describes the gesture of Bartimaeus the blind man who rises quickly after hearing Jesus' call. The context emphasizes the urgency and eagerness of the character: despite his blindness, he does not ask to be guided; he leaps towards Jesus. This choice of verb reinforces the impression of liveliness and fervent faith of the character.
G6008.portee: This word shows us how to respond to Jesus' call: without calculation, without hesitation, rising with eagerness to meet Him. Bartimaeus' leap becomes an image of the promptness and fervor that the disciple should have in their faith.

sens: Sharp point, especially that of a weapon
Sewing needle
What is fine and narrow, by comparison
G6011.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a sharp and cutting point: it is the tip of a spear or a weapon of war. This image conveys both finesse and primary danger.
2. A sewing needle, the ordinary instrument for piercing and assembling fabrics. This is the sense that Jesus uses in his famous saying: "It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God" (Luke 18:25). The image contrasts the camel, the largest and heaviest animal of the desert, with the tiny eye of the needle.
3. By extension, anything that is extremely fine, narrow, or difficult to pass through. The needle becomes the image of an almost impossible passage.
G6011.origine: The Greek word belonē comes from bélos, which means "dart" or "missile weapon." It belongs to a family of words concerning projectiles and sharp objects. The root evokes the idea of "piercing" or "penetrating." What begins as a fearsome weapon becomes, by the same trait of finesse, a tool of everyday life.
G6011.emploi: Belonē appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 18:25. Jesus uses it in a parable to illustrate the impossible: how could a rich man enter the kingdom of God? It is as if a camel were trying to pass through the eye of a needle. The evangelists Matthew and Mark report the same saying, but with a nearby Greek word (rhapis). In Luke, the needle embodies the extreme limit of what is achievable, the visible absurdity.
G6011.portee: This image of the camel and the needle reveals how wealth can become an obstacle to faith. It speaks not only of money but of what burdens us and distances us from God. The needle, so fine, reminds us that the passage to the kingdom requires becoming light, stripped, and available. It is an invitation to rethink our relationship with material goods.

sens: The harvested product of a plant, particularly from the vine
Metaphorically, the result or effect of an action, work, or virtue
G6013.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the fruit that is harvested, especially the grape from the vine. Jesus uses this image when speaking of the "fruit of the vine" — it is the wine, the finished product of the grape — to evoke the moment when he will no longer drink until the meal of the kingdom (Matthew 26:29; Mark 14:25; Luke 22:18). It is the concrete product that the vine yields.
2. Figuratively, the word is used to denote the visible results of a state or virtue. Thus, in 2 Corinthians 9:10, Paul speaks of the "fruits of your righteousness": just as the earth produces a harvest, a person's righteousness produces visible results in the world.
G6013.origine: The word γένημα comes from the root γεν- (gén-), which expresses the idea of "to generate, produce, give birth to." The same root is found in γεννάω (to generate, give birth) and γέννημα (that which is generated). The word literally means "that which is produced" or "that which is born of." In Hebrew, the idea is found in words like פְּרִי (péri, fruit) which have the same concrete and figurative scope.
G6013.emploi: This word appears four times in the New Testament, always in Greek. Three uses are found in the first three Gospels where Jesus speaks of the "fruit of the vine" during the Last Supper, with slightly different formulations but the same meaning. The fourth use, in 2 Corinthians 9:10, moves from the agricultural domain to apply the image to moral and spiritual life: the "fruits" of righteousness are the benefits and concrete results it produces. The meaning thus oscillates between material fruit and spiritual fruit, metaphorically.
G6013.portee: This word invites the reader to see the continuity between the material world and the spiritual world. Just as a vine produces fruit, a righteous life produces visible results. Jesus himself uses the image of fruit to speak of expectation and fulfillment: he looks forward to drinking new wine in the kingdom. This reminds us that our righteousness, like a seed, bears fruit — not by our own strength, but because God cultivates it.

sens: Fear mixed with respect in the face of something great and sacred
Feeling of attachment to God accompanied by reverence and caution
G6015.detail:
1. Reverent fear is that fear which arises before what is great, sacred, and worthy of respect. It is not a fear that paralyzes or causes one to flee, but a fear that restrains, that makes one bow their head, that inspires respect. It is the feeling someone experiences in the presence of majesty or formidable power.
2. In the Bible, this feeling is directed towards God himself. When we receive from God an unshakeable kingdom, we must serve him with "reverent fear," according to Hebrews 12:28. This means that our worship must be accompanied by a respectful awareness of divine holiness and a certain pious vigilance — what the Bible also calls "piety" or "attachment to God."
G6015.origine: The word comes from the Greek root δείδω (deidô), which means "to dread, to fear." It is a feeling that is older and deeper than simple fear: it is the fear that seizes one before the divine, the majestic, the sacred. The biblical context shows that it is a positive fear, one that leads the worshiper to serve God with respect and vigilance.
G6015.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 12:28. The apostle uses it to exhort Christians who have received an unshakeable kingdom to render to God a "pleasing" worship — that is, worship accompanied by reverent fear and piety. The word emphasizes that our relationship with God must never lose this dimension of respect and conscious attachment to his holiness, even after being justified by faith.
G6015.portee: Understanding the reverent fear of the Lord is essential for the believer: it is not the enemy of joy or trust in God, but its foundation. It preserves Christian worship from superficiality and carnal familiarity, and keeps the worshiper in conscious humility before divine majesty. It makes worship a true, serious, and living act at the same time.

sens: Remove all dirt or impurities from a surface or place
In an agricultural sense, completely separate the grain from the chaff
Figuratively, purify or refine something thoroughly
G6016.detail: 1. The verb describes the action of thoroughly cleaning, removing all traces of dirt or impurity. It is a cleaning that leaves nothing dirty: scrubbing, rubbing until everything is clean. In Luke 3:17, John the Baptist describes the Messiah who will "clean" his threshing floor completely — that is, he will separate the good grain from the bad grain, leaving no mixture. 2. In the agricultural context, the "cleaning" of the threshing floor means harvesting according to the rules: using the winnowing fan (a tool for sifting), removing everything that is not grain, and storing the good grain in the barn. It is a complete work of sorting and purification. 3. The image can take on a spiritual meaning: the one who "cleans" completely acts as a purifier, a figure of judgment and justice. The impurities removed represent evil or guilt that cannot be ignored.
G6016.origine: The verb is composed of the Greek prefix "dia" (through, completely) and "kathairō" (to clean, to purify). This composition reinforces the idea of depth and totality: it is not a simple cleaning, but a complete and systematic cleaning. The root "kathairō" evokes the idea of removing what is pure from what is not, a clear separation.
G6016.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 3:17. John the Baptist uses it when speaking of the coming Messiah, of whom he is not worthy to untie the sandal. The image of threshing — cleaning the floor — is a parable of judgment: the Messiah will separate the righteous (the grain stored in the barn) from the unrighteous (the chaff burned in the fire). This passage shows how the word applies not only to a material and agricultural act but also to the messianic work of sorting and final purification of God's people.
G6016.portee: This word reminds Christians that God's judgment is not approximate or partial: it is a complete cleaning, a definitive separation between what remains (the grain) and what will be destroyed (the chaff). It also invites reflection on one's own position in this divine sorting — am I grain or chaff? — and on the reality of final judgment, not merely as a threat but as the fulfillment of God's justice.

sens: To ridicule someone by making fun of them
To publicly deride
To refuse to believe or take seriously
G6017.detail:
1. To mock means to ridicule someone or something by making fun of them, often with a tone of contempt or irony. It is to show insolence through words, seeking to humiliate or make others laugh at someone else's expense. In Acts 2:13, after the disciples receive the Holy Spirit and speak in tongues, some bystanders "mocked" them, saying they were drunk on sweet wine: a public derision intended to discredit what had just happened.
2. The word emphasizes an intense mockery, where one does not simply joke: one actively seeks to ridicule someone. It is taking pleasure in belittling others.
3. To mock can also express a refusal to take seriously, to believe, or to respect. The mockers in Acts 2 immediately rejected the extraordinary testimony they were hearing.
G6017.origine: The Greek word διαχλευάζω (diachleuazō) is composed of the prefix δια- (dia-, "through", "intensely") and χλευάζω (chleuzō, "to mock, to ridicule"). The prefix makes the verb more intense and pronounced: it is not a simple joke, but a deliberate and pronounced mockery. The root χλευάζω itself evokes the idea of malicious laughter or sarcasm. It is a verb of hostile action through words.
G6017.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 2:13, at the key moment of Pentecost. There, spectators mock the apostles who are speaking in tongues, claiming they are simply drunk. This mockery reveals the unbelieving heart: faced with a miracle, some choose to ridicule rather than seek to understand. The context shows that mockery is often the reaction of those who refuse to acknowledge the work of the Holy Spirit. It is a verb that describes open hostility towards faith.
G6017.portee: Recognizing this word invites the reader to see how mockery and rejection manifest in the face of spiritual realities. Pentecost could have converted these spectators, but they preferred to mock. This reminds us that unbelief often expresses itself through irony and ridicule: to mock becomes a veil that prevents seeing. For the Christian, it is a warning against the temptation to ridicule what one does not understand, and a lesson on the humble astonishment that God's action should inspire.

sens: To mentally examine, weigh in one's mind
To meditate on something to understand it
To carefully consider a troubling vision or event
G6018.detail:
1. To reflect means to examine something in one's mind, to turn it over and over in thought. Peter, after having the strange vision of unclean animals, reflected on what it could mean (Acts 10:19): he does not immediately understand and wonders, "What does this mean?"
2. It is also to meditate, to weigh the pros and cons, to let one's mind work on a question. The word suggests not an immediate understanding, but a mental process where one tries to make sense of something difficult or unexpected.
3. It is to consider, to be immersed in one's thoughts — an attitude of inner concentration that can last for a while, where one sees and hears only what one is reflecting on.
G6018.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: "dia" (through) and "enthuméomai" (to consider, to have in mind). The primary image is to let something pass through one's mind, to mentally traverse it. It is a verb of inner activity, of thorough mental examination.
G6018.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament Greek, in Peter's account in Acts 10. Peter has just received a vision from heaven where unclean animals are presented to him, and he reflects on what this means — it is a moment of spiritual perplexity. It is at this precise moment that the Spirit speaks to him to explain that the vision concerns the inclusion of Gentiles in salvation.
G6018.portee: This word shows us that even the apostles had to reflect, meditate, and allow time for the Spirit to clarify His will. Spiritual reflection is not unbelief: it is an honest pause in the face of mystery, an openness to God for Him to instruct us.

sens: The action of putting someone to the test, assessing their reaction
The trial endured, that which tests faith or loyalty
The presentation of verifiable facts to verify the truth of a statement
G6020.detail:
1. This word refers to the act of testing something or someone: submitting to a trial to see if it holds up, if it works, if it can be trusted. In Hebrews 3:9, the fathers of Israel sought to test God Himself for forty years in the desert, trying to see if He would keep His promises or abandon them.
2. The trial itself, the difficult experience that tests faith. It is what happens to someone to verify the quality of their trust or loyalty towards God.
G6020.origine: The word comes from the verb δοκιμάζω (dokimazô: to examine, to test, to approve), which evokes the image of a metallurgist or assayer testing gold or silver to verify their quality. This same root produces other biblical words describing examination or testing: it always speaks of a serious and methodical verification, as when one wants to know if something is true or reliable.
G6020.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 3:9, where it refers to the moment in the desert when the children of Israel tested God. There is irony here: the Israelites, instead of trusting God and allowing Him to test them to refine their faith, allowed themselves to doubt Him and sought to 'test' Him. The context shows that this 'test' was a mark of their unbelief and rebellion, not a righteous endeavor.
G6020.portee: This passage teaches us that our doubts about God's faithfulness constitute a testing of His person — we are, in a sense, testing Him, as if we doubted that He speaks the truth. This image, just before the call to enter into God's rest, exhorts us to change our posture: instead of putting God to the test through our unbelief, we are to trust Him so that His Word and His works test us and strengthen us in faith.

sens: To speak ill of someone, tarnishing their reputation with malicious or false words
To be the object of slander, to suffer unjust verbal attacks
G6022.detail: 1. To slander means to speak ill of someone, deliberately and maliciously, to tarnish their reputation and discredit them. It involves making unjust accusations or reproaches. Paul uses it to describe what the Corinthians are enduring: they are spoken ill of without reason, insulted, and belittled. 2. In the passive form (to be slandered), the word describes the one who receives these malicious verbal attacks: they are the victim. In 1 Corinthians 4:13, Paul states that the apostles 'are slandered' but respond with gentleness and kindness, showing that enduring slander should not cause us to lose our charity.
G6022.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: 'dys' (bad, difficulty) and 'phêmê' (word, rumor). It literally means 'bad word' or 'bad reputation'. This compound expresses the idea of negative words that spread and damage someone's honor. The passive form, found in 1 Corinthians 4:13, emphasizes the experience of the one who suffers these attacks.
G6022.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 4:13, in the passive form. Paul uses it to express the sufferings and insults that the apostles endure for the Gospel. He places this slander among the trials that faithful Christians must face ('slandered, we speak with kindness'), which shows that slander is a common persecution against the disciples of Christ. The context emphasizes the humble and loving response that should be given.
G6022.portee: Slander is a weapon of evil: it hurts, isolates, and distorts the truth. But Paul teaches us that being slandered is not a shame — it is a trial even the apostles endure — and that our strength does not depend on what others say about us, but on our faithfulness to the Gospel. In the face of slander, the Christian is called to respond 'with kindness', maintaining integrity rather than seeking revenge through words.

sens: The act of questioning, debating
A subject that provokes dispute or controversy
Unproductive debate, vain argumentation
G6027.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the action of asking questions, interrogating, or debating: it is questioning to seek understanding or to discuss.

2. It refers to a subject or matter that provokes dispute and disagreement among people. In 1 Timothy 1:4, Paul targets endless genealogies that become subjects of endless debate.

3. The meaning can also lean towards 'discussion' in the sense of a hollow and useless debate: the emphasis is then on the vain, unproductive nature of the debate — it distracts from what truly matters, namely the advancement of God's work.
G6027.origine: The word comes from the verb ἐκζητέω (ekzēteō), formed from ἐκ (ek, 'out of', intensive) and ζητέω (zēteō, 'to seek, to search'). The basic idea is thus one of 'searching that goes beyond', of an 'intense quest' or deep questioning. In this context, it takes on a negative connotation: a search, a quest that strays from the true goal.
G6027.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 1:4. Paul uses it to warn against debates that divide the assembly and distract from the true purpose of ministry. He specifically targets endless genealogies and fables — subjects that fuel quarrels rather than authentic faith and mutual edification. The apostle thus distinguishes what builds the Christian community (the work of God, the administration of faith) from what paralyzes it (the 'discussions' that are endless and sterile).
G6027.portee: This word teaches us that the Christian faith is not meant for endless quarrels, but for action and spiritual growth. It urges us to discern between sincere seeking of the truth and hollow debate that divides the Church. It invites the believer to prefer what edifies, what advances God's work, over what lulls the assembly into endless controversies.

sens: To be surprised and filled with admiration or perplexity before something unexpected
To experience a form of astonishment mixed with trouble or uncertainty
G6028.detail:
1. It is to be taken by surprise and struck by something that exceeds expectations, to the point of being filled with admiration or perplexity. In Mark 12:17, when Jesus responds to the Pharisees about the tribute to Caesar by saying 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's', they remain 'astonished' — that is, dumbfounded, unable to reply, impressed by the wisdom of the answer.
2. The word expresses a particular force of astonishment, an emotion or trouble mixed with admiration. It is not a mere fleeting surprise, but a profound astonishment that leaves the person speechless.
G6028.origine: The word is formed from the intensifying prefix 'ek' ('out of') added to the root 'thaumazô' ('to be astonished'). This combination creates a reinforced form, signaling a stronger, more manifest astonishment — literally, 'to be astonished out of oneself'. The simple root 'thaumazô' already expresses wonder and surprise, very common in the New Testament; the prefix marks it as particularly intense.
G6028.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 12:17. It is a word from biblical language and deuterocanonical writings, less common than its simple form. It describes the precise state of Jesus' adversaries after His brilliant retort to the Pharisees and Herodians: they cannot contradict Him or trap Him, and remain struck with astonishment. The use of the reinforced word emphasizes the intensity of their amazement at this wisdom.
G6028.portee: This moment reveals that the wisdom of Jesus leaves those who seek to quarrel with Him speechless. For the believer, it reminds us that the word of Jesus has a power that disarms closed minds and compels admiration even from those who reject Him. It is a lesson on the strength of truth spoken with authority.

sens: To suddenly leap forward
To launch oneself forcefully towards something
To dash with urgency and impulsiveness
G6030.detail:
1. The word describes the movement of someone who suddenly leaps or springs forward, like a spring that releases. It is an instinctive and quick gesture. In Acts 14:14, Paul and Barnabas rush into the crowd to stop the idolatrous worship that begins towards them.

2. It is also the action of launching oneself forcefully towards a destination, driven by a strong emotion — here alarm and apostolic zeal. The movement is not reflective: it conveys an immediate reaction of the heart.

3. The word suggests urgency, even impetuosity: one does not go step by step, but rushes. This shows how disturbed Paul and Barnabas were to see the crowds wanting to worship them, and how they acted without delay.
G6030.origine: The word combines the prefix "ek" (out of, outside) and "pēdaō" (to leap, to spring). This root evokes the image of a sudden and energetic movement, like that of an animal jumping. Neighboring verbs in Greek describe all sudden movements: to gush forth water, to rush into battle. The Greek Old Testament notably uses it to translate the Hebrew verb "zanaq" (to leap, to spring) in Deuteronomy 33:22, describing Levi who rushes into battle.
G6030.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: Acts 14:14. Paul and Barnabas, received as gods by the crowd of Lystra, tear their clothes and rush into the midst of the people to stop them and cry out that this worship must cease. The use of the word shows the urgency and emotion of the moment — there is no hesitation, just a protective and passionate reaction from the apostles. This rare verb emphasizes the sudden and irresistible nature of their gesture.
G6030.portee: This word reveals how Paul and Barnabas, far from seeking glory, risk their lives to preserve the honor of God. Their rushing is not thoughtless impulsiveness, but zeal — the burning love of God propels them forward. For the Christian, this raises the question: am I ready to react with such urgency when God's honor is at stake?

sens: The act of convincing someone of their error or sin
The state of being convinced, being confronted with the truth
Reproach or correction addressed to someone who has acted wrongly
G6031.detail:
1. It is the act of showing someone that they are wrong, that they have made a mistake or committed a sin. In 2 Timothy 3:16, Paul says that Scripture is useful for "convincing": it shows the reader their errors and faults.
2. It is also the result of this action: the person is then convinced, they recognize their error or sin in the face of the truth. It is a realization imposed by confrontation with reality.
3. More broadly, it is the reproach or correction itself, the words or actions by which one makes someone understand that they have acted wrongly. It is a strong word: it is not just about criticizing, but about bringing to light guilt.
G6031.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ἐλέγχω (elegchô), which means "to convince" or "to refute". It denotes the action of showing in the light, of highlighting. The root evokes the idea of making the truth clear, particularly the truth of an accusation or sin. In the Greek Old Testament, the same word translates the Hebrew תּוֹכֵחָה (tôkéḥâh), which means "reprimand" or "correction."
G6031.emploi: This word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:16. Paul lists the uses of Scripture: it "convicts" people of their sins and errors. This is one of the major roles of the Word of God: it does not simply instruct or advise, it exposes and reveals guilt. The context shows that this function of conviction is indispensable, alongside teaching, correction, and instruction in righteousness.
G6031.portee: This word reminds the believer that the Bible is not just a manual of pleasant advice: it is a living word that clearly exposes our sins and errors. This is good news, for being convicted of one's sin is the path to repentance and reconciliation with God. For the one who listens to the Word, conviction becomes an act of divine love.

sens: Mocking, derisive ridicule
Words or behavior that mock someone or something
G6032.detail:
1. Mockery is an open derision of someone or something, often with the intention to hurt or ridicule. In 2 Peter 3:3, the apostle speaks of "mockers" who will come "with their mockeries": they will mock God's promises and the return of Christ, denying the reality of future judgment and living according to their carnal desires.
2. It is a word or attitude that ridicules, belittles, or refuses to take seriously. In this biblical context, the mockery of the last days' scoffers expresses their contemptuous refusal to believe in God's word and warnings.
G6032.origine: The word comes from the root "empaizô" (to mock, to ridicule), composed of "em-" (in, with) and "paizô" (to play, to jest). It is primarily "to play against" someone, then "to mock." Mockery thus expresses a cruel game: one plays with someone to turn them into a joke.
G6032.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 3:3. Peter uses it to describe the behavior of false teachers and ungodly men of the last days: they mock the promises of Christ, deny future judgment, and live in ungodliness. It is a mockery characterized by contempt for revealed truth and refusal to submit one's life to God.
G6032.portee: For the Christian, this mention reminds us that contempt for faith is not new and will intensify before the return of Christ. It invites us not to be surprised or discouraged by the mockery of the unbelievers, but to remain steadfast in faith in the fulfillment of God's promises.

sens: This place, this specific point where one stands
From here, from this side
From this place from which one speaks
G6033.detail:
1. "Here" designates the place where the speaker stands or the immediate space being referred to. In Matthew 17:20, Jesus tells his disciples to command the mountain "from here" — that is, from the point where you are now, from the ground where you stand — to go there. The adverb marks the starting point, the concrete here of the speaker.
2. "Here" can also mean "from this side" or "from this side here." In Luke 16:26, Abraham says "from here to you" — that is, from the side where we are (within Abraham, in paradise) to your side (in Hades). The adverb indicates a movement that starts from this specific place to another.
G6033.origine: The Greek word ἔνθεν comes from a very ancient root that expresses the idea of "there, at that place." It is related to ἐκεῖ ("there") and ὅθεν ("from where"). It is a demonstrative adverb that points to a place very concretely, as if the speaker is saying "you see, right here." Greek poets (Homer, notably) used it to designate a place or a side in a spatial direction.
G6033.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both directly related to a space or place. In Matthew 17:20, Jesus uses it to tell the disciples where the command given to the mountain should start: from here where you are. In Luke 16:26, Abraham uses it to describe the opposite sides of a great chasm, separating the living from the dead. In both cases, the adverb remains very spatial, very concrete: it anchors the discourse in a specific place, that from which one speaks or from which the movement begins.
G6033.portee: This small word reminds us that Jesus speaks to his disciples in a real situation: he places them face to face with the mountain, here, now. It also teaches us that faith is never abstract — it is exercised "from here where you are." The word of God does not require us to move elsewhere to obey: it asks us to act from the point where we find ourselves. It is an invitation to concrete trust, rooted in the present.

sens: to make someone swear, to solemnly ask someone to do something in the name of God or a sacred authority
G6034.detail: 1. Conjure means to address someone with a very solemn request, invoking them in the name of God or a sacred power. It is to place someone under an obligation to do something by the weight of an oath or the respect due to God. In 1 Thessalonians 5:27, Paul conjures the faithful "by the Lord" to have his letter read to all the brothers: he is not simply expressing a wish, but issuing a command imbued with divine authority.
G6034.origine: The Greek word comes from the prefix "en" (in) and "orki" (oath, sacred thing): to conjure is literally to "place someone in the oath." The corresponding Hebrew word in the Greek Old Testament is "chaba" in the causative form (hi.), which also means to make someone swear or to compel by oath. This root evokes the idea of binding someone by a sacred word.
G6034.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament (1 Thessalonians 5:27). Paul uses it to urge the Thessalonians with a solemn obligation: that his letter be read publicly to the entire assembly. The context shows that Paul clothes his request with religious authority by invoking the Lord, signaling the critical importance of the message and guaranteeing its apostolic nature. It is a pastoral use where the conjuration serves to strengthen the obedience and unity of the church.
G6034.portee: This word reminds the Christian that certain words, certain pastoral or apostolic orders carry an authority that transcends mere human persuasion. When Paul conjures the faithful in the name of the Lord, he calls them to obey not out of fear or coercion, but by recognizing that the apostolic Word bears the mark of the divine. For today's reader, this invites a respectful consideration of the solemn calls of Scripture and spiritual leaders based on the truth of God.

sens: Struck by a divine curse or solemnly condemned
Rejected or despised as unworthy of favor
G6035.detail:
1. The word designates one upon whom a curse weighs — someone whom God has devoted to judgment or who has been solemnly delivered to condemnation. It is the state of being cursed, that is, being under the weight of a contrary divine sentence. In John 7:49, the religious leaders despise the crowd by calling them "cursed": they mean that these people, ignorant of the law, are excluded from divine favor and worthy of contempt.
2. By extension, the word can designate one who is rejected or considered unworthy — not always due to a formal curse, but because they are regarded as despicable or excluded from good and blessing.
G6035.origine: The word comes from the verb ἐπαράομαι (to invoke a curse upon someone) and carries the prefix ἐπί which reinforces the idea: it is someone upon whom a curse has been invoked or pronounced. The root evokes the act of cursing, that is, wishing or pronouncing evil against someone. It is the opposite of "blessed": where blessing brings favor and life, cursing brings judgment and rejection.
G6035.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament (John 7:49), in the mouths of the religious leaders of the Sanhedrin despising the crowd. They label as "cursed" those who are ignorant of the law — not that the crowd is actually cursed by God, but because the leaders consider them unworthy, excluded from true knowledge and thus from blessing. It is a word of social and religious contempt, a condemnation pronounced by the authorities against those they deem inferior.
G6035.portee: This verse invites the Christian to reflect on the judgment we cast upon others. The religious leaders believed themselves authorized to exclude and condemn those who did not share their knowledge. Yet Jesus defends the simple crowd and shows that true condemnation and true blessing come from God alone, not from human judgment based on social status or formal religious knowledge.

sens: To arrive suddenly beside someone or something
To occur unexpectedly or inevitably
G6036.detail:
1. The word depicts the sudden arrival and approach of a threat or significant event: there is the idea of movement directed precisely toward someone. In Luke 21:35, the Day of the Lord "will come" like a trap upon all the inhabitants of the earth — that is, it will fall upon them, encompassing them unexpectedly.
2. By extension, it designates anything that occurs inevitably, often without one being able to truly avoid or prepare for it. It is an event that imposes itself upon us, whether we expect it or not.
G6036.origine: The word combines three elements: ἐπί (upon, against), εἰς (toward, into) and ἔρχομαι (to come, to go). This composition creates the image of a directed arrival, a coming that happens "upon" someone, with the force of the unexpected. It is a verb formed to express not just a simple passing, but an arrival that affects the one toward whom it is directed.
G6036.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 21:35, in Jesus' apocalyptic discourse about the end times. Jesus warns his disciples that the Day of judgment "will come" like a snare upon those who live on the whole earth, without them expecting it. It is a term chosen to emphasize the inevitable nature and the element of surprise of this event.
G6036.portee: This word invites the reader to take seriously Jesus' warning: God's judgment will not be distant or theoretical, but real and immediate for those who are unprepared. It calls for vigilance and obedience, for the events of world history and our lives can occur without warning.

sens: To put seeds on the ground or among other plants
To plant secretly, in hiding
G6037.detail:
1. The verb primarily means the action of spreading seeds on a field, particularly throwing them among other crops. It is the gesture of the sower in a field. In Matthew 13:25, the enemy "sows" tares among the wheat: he throws the bad seeds directly into the field already sown with good grain.
2. The word takes on a malevolent shade when the action is done in secret, while no one is watching. It is not an ordinary seed, but a corruption slipped in stealthily. The enemy acts "while people slept": it is the image of cunning, of hidden sabotage.
G6037.origine: The word combines the prefix "epi" (upon, above) and the verb "speirô" (to sow). The image is that of throwing something over, adding a seed to another. The root "speirô" is that of the sower and the grain; it also appears in "spérma" (seed, offspring). It is a rare verb in the New Testament.
G6037.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in Matthew 13:25, in the parable of the wheat and the tares. Jesus tells how a man sows good grain in his field, but during the night, his enemy comes and sows tares among the wheat. The context reveals that this action is voluntary, malevolent, and hidden: it is an act of agricultural sabotage. The parable then unfolds into spiritual explanation.
G6037.portee: This parable teaches the believer that evil often settles secretly in the world and in the Church, mixed with good, and that the final separation of the two will only come at the final judgment. It also invites vigilance: the sleep of the servants (inattention) allows the enemy to act. It is a call to remain spiritually awake.

sens: Show passion, fervor for something or someone
Be zealous in one's convictions, religious commitments
Seek intensely to please or serve
G6041.detail:
1. Zeal is an ardor, a passion that drives one to act intensely. It is an inner force that compels one to give oneself entirely to what one does. In Revelation 3:19, Christ calls the church of Laodicea to be zealous: it is not enough to believe half-heartedly; one must burn with passion for one's faith and to please the Lord.
2. Zeal can also refer to ardent jealousy, the desire not to share what one cherishes. It is an intense feeling that can be good when directed towards God — jealous for His honor, His purity — or bad when it becomes envy or carnal jealousy.
3. In a spiritual sense, to have zeal means to put all one's energy into serving God and living according to His commandments, with sincere and fervent commitment rather than with lukewarmness.
G6041.origine: This verb comes from ζηλόω (zēlóō), which denotes ardor and passion. The root evokes the image of heat, of boiling — something that bubbles internally. Zeal is a force that consumes, that revives. It is the word found when the Bible speaks of the fervor of Christ or the passionate commitment of believers.
G6041.emploi: The verb is rare in the New Testament: there is only one certain occurrence in Revelation 3:19, where Jesus exhorts the church to shake off its spiritual lukewarmness. The context shows that the zeal He speaks of is not a superficial agitation, but a return to passion, to sincere commitment. It is the antidote to religious mediocrity, to the attitude of the 'almost Christian' who does not truly commit to anything.
G6041.portee: For the Christian, this passage invites deep reflection: am I lukewarm or fervent in my faith? Biblical zeal is not fanaticism, but the ardor of one who has truly encountered God and desires to please Him with all their heart. It is a call not to settle for a routine faith, but to live with passion and sincerity in one's commitment to Christ.

sens: ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke
G6043.detail: Joda is an ancestor of Jesus mentioned only once in the genealogy established by Luke. He is the father of Maath and is situated several generations before Jesus, in the lineage that traces back from Joseph, the husband of Mary.
G6043.origine: The name Joda is a Greek form of a Hebrew name. It is a masculine name that belongs to the tradition of Jewish patriarchal names. The text of Luke uses the Greek form Ἰώδα (Iôda) to include this character in a complete genealogy.
G6043.emploi: Joda appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:26, where he is listed in the genealogy of Jesus. He is identified as the father of Maath and the son of Mattathias. This genealogy differs from that of Matthew, showing the various ancestral traditions preserved in early Christian circles.

sens: figure of the first century
ancestor of Jesus according to the genealogy of Luke
G6044.detail: Josech is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogy of Jesus presented by Luke. He lived a few generations before Jesus and was the son of Maath and the father of Joëda. This genealogy traces the lineage of Jesus from His childhood back to Adam, thus showing that Jesus belongs to the human lineage according to God's plan.
G6044.origine: Josech is a Hebrew (or Aramaic) name borne by this member of the Davidic genealogy. Although its precise meaning is uncertain, this type of name was common in Israel during the centuries before the Christian era. The name appears in the genealogical list that Luke reproduces, reflecting Jewish traditions regarding family descent.
G6044.emploi: Josech appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:26. He is included in the genealogy that Luke presents after the baptism of Jesus, tracing back generation by generation to Adam. This genealogy is distinct from that reported by Matthew; it shows Luke's concern to situate Jesus in the history of the people of Israel and to demonstrate that the Messiah truly comes from humanity.

sens: In the same way as, just as
Expresses a comparison of equality or similarity
Introduces a concrete example that illustrates the point
G6045.detail:
1. This word introduces a comparison: it means 'in the same way as' or 'just as'. In Hebrews 5:4, it establishes a parallel between the calling of the high priest and that of Aaron: no one takes this honor upon himself unless called by God, 'just as' Aaron was.
2. It expresses a similarity or equality between two realities: what happened to one also applies to the other. It is a way to strengthen an argument by showing that a present situation resembles a previous or known situation.
3. The comparison it marks is never vague: it focuses on a specific point and serves to clarify or justify what has just been said. Here, the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews uses it to affirm that no one can become a high priest without divine calling, relying on the historical example of Aaron.
G6045.origine: This word is composed of καθώς ('as'), which already expresses comparison, reinforced by the particle περ, which adds a nuance of intensity or precision ('even', 'just'). Together, they form a very marked conjunction of comparison. The corresponding Hebrew word in the Old Testament is often כַּאֲשֶׁר ('as', 'according to'), which expresses the same logical function of parallel or resemblance.
G6045.emploi: This word appears very rarely in the New Testament (only in Hebrews 5:4 in the major manuscripts). It belongs to the formal and argumentative style of doctrinal epistles. The author uses it to support his theological reasoning on the apostolic calling of Christ: by comparing the dignity of Christ to that of Aaron, he shows that every minister established by God receives their charge by divine calling, never by usurpation. This comparison reinforces the legitimacy of Christ's position as high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.
G6045.portee: This word teaches us the importance of the divine foundation of spiritual authority. It reminds us that Christian ministry is never a personal conquest or a human pretense, but a calling from God. By showing the parallel with Aaron, the text tells us that every faithful minister, like Christ Himself, must receive their mission from God. This establishes the believer's confidence: our spiritual responsibilities are legitimate only if they come from God.

sens: Make heavy, weigh down physically
Burden someone, overwhelm them
Thicken or numb the eyes, making them heavy with sleep
G6046.detail:
1. The verb means to make heavy, to weigh down, as if throwing a weight on something. It is the image of a burden that weighs and slows down.
2. Figuratively, it describes the effect of a moral or physical burden that crushes someone, overloading or oppressing them.
3. In Mark 14:40, the word precisely describes the eyes of the disciples asleep in Gethsemane: their eyelids have become heavy, numb from sleep, unable to stay open. The apostle John recounts how Jesus finds them asleep a second time, "for their eyes were heavy." This is not voluntary laziness, but the physical effect of fatigue weighing on them.
G6046.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that means heavy or weighty (βαρύς, barys). The prefix κατα (kata) reinforces the idea by adding the notion of an action that acts downward, which burdens. It is a common formation in Greek: one adds "kata" to an adjective to make it an action verb. The corresponding Hebrew word in the Greek Old Testament is often כָּבַד (kabad), which also means to be heavy or to weigh down.
G6046.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 14:40. It is used in the account of Jesus' agony in Gethsemane, when the three disciples Peter, James, and John fall asleep despite the Lord's warnings. The use of the verb "appesantir" highlights the poignant contrast: the disciples, who were supposed to watch and pray, are overcome by physical sleep at the very moment Jesus faces his greatest spiritual trial.
G6046.portee: This word reminds readers of human weakness in the face of God's calls. The disciples were not malicious, but overwhelmed by a physical fatigue they could not control — an image of our condition: we want to pray and remain vigilant, but we discover how fragile and spiritually drowsy we are. The passage invites us to recognize our need for God's grace rather than relying on our own strength.

sens: judgment pronouncing guilt and penalty
hostile judicial verdict
decision of a court against someone
G6048.detail:
1. Condemnation is the judgment of a court that declares someone guilty and sentences them to a penalty. In Acts 25:15, the Jewish leaders request Paul's condemnation before the Roman governor: they want an official verdict declaring him guilty and punishing him.
2. It is primarily a concrete judicial act — a sentence pronounced publicly by one who has authority. The word evokes the weight of a legal decision that falls upon the accused.
3. By extension, it designates any hostile decision from an authority that judges and strikes. It is a serious word, carrying the meaning of "judgment against" someone.
G6048.origine: The Greek word is composed of *kata* ("against, upon") and *dikē* ("judgment, justice, right"). It literally means "judgment-against." The root *dikē* evokes the idea of justice and retribution; the prefix *kata* reinforces the sense of an action directed against someone. The word emphasizes that the judgment falls upon the accused like a blow.
G6048.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 25:15. Paul stands before the Roman governor Festus; the Jewish leaders demand a *condemnation* against him — in other words, they insist that Festus declare him guilty. It is a legal term that underscores the political and religious stakes of the trial: the Jews want an official sentence. The context shows that this requested condemnation is unjust, as Paul has done nothing to warrant such a penalty.
G6048.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that condemnation is the price of sin — and that only Jesus has paid this price in our place. By reading how Paul refuses the unjust condemnation in Acts, we also see that divine judgment is just and merciful for those who believe in Christ.

sens: Bless with a particular intensity
Invoke divine blessing on someone with fervor and tenderness
G6050.detail: 1. The word expresses a blessing that is not merely spoken but given with strength and warmth. Mark 10:16 shows Jesus who "blesses" the little children by taking them in his arms and laying his hands on them — each gesture reinforces the intensity of the act of blessing. 2. This ardent blessing is that of a father or a leader who earnestly desires to convey divine favor, manifesting it through his physical and emotional engagement. It is to bless, not casually, but by personally committing to the well-being of the one being blessed.
G6050.origine: The word is formed from the Greek prefix κατά (kata, "downward, intensely") and ευλογέω (eulogeō, "to bless"). This prefix reinforces the basic idea: instead of simply blessing, one blesses in a strong, complete, invested manner. The Greek word εὐλογία (eulogia, "blessing") has the same root: it literally means "good word," since ευ (eu) means "good" and λόγος (logos) means "word." To bless, therefore, is to address a good word, and "to bless with ardor" is to give it with all one's heart.
G6050.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 10:16. Jesus, surrounded by disciples who wanted to dismiss the little children, rebukes them, then welcomes them tenderly: he "blesses" them by taking them in his arms and laying his hands on them. It is a moment of explicitly warm and embodied blessing, quite different from a mere formula. The context indicates that this blessing is an act of love and protection towards the smallest.
G6050.portee: This word reveals Jesus' blessing as an act full of warmth and intention. When Jesus blesses, he does not speak from afar: he draws near, he touches, he engages. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize that divine blessing is never cold or distant — it comes from a God who truly cares for us and desires our good with all his heart.

sens: one who brings an accusation, who denounces someone
one who seeks to have someone condemned, to discredit
in a spiritual sense: Satan as he accuses believers before God
G6051.detail:
1. An accuser is one who files a complaint, who denounces a fault or a crime before a judge or authority. It is a person who accuses someone else. In Revelation 12:10, the term refers to Satan as the one who presents believers in their worst light before God, day and night.
2. The role of an accuser implies an intention to do harm: not only to state what one believes to be true, but to desire the condemnation or downfall of the accused. Satan is described as the quintessential accuser of Christ's disciples, always seeking to discredit them before their Heavenly Father.
3. Spiritually, this word reveals an invisible dimension of the Christian struggle. Satan does not have the power to directly destroy redeemed believers, but he constantly accuses them, fills them with guilt, and drives them to despair by reminding them of their past or present sins, as if to separate them from the love of God.
G6051.origine: The Greek word κατήγωρ comes from a verb meaning "to speak against, to accuse." It is closely related to κατήγορος, a more common form, which designates the accuser in trials. The form κατήγωρ itself comes from the Aramaic קָטִיגוֺר (qatīgōr), a legal borrowing used in Eastern legal contexts. This root expresses the idea of a word directed against someone to accuse them.
G6051.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 12:10. It is a hapax, meaning a very rare form. The context is that of a heavenly vision where heaven is filled with praise after the eschatological defeat of Satan. The Apostle John uses this term specifically to identify Satan: not merely as an enemy or destroyer, but as an accuser, one who judges and condemns believers. Revelation emphasizes that Satan "accused them before our God day and night" — an image of his incessant and malevolent activity aimed at discrediting and condemning Christ's disciples.
G6051.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals how Satan operates: not by brute force, but through accusation, guilt, and despair. Understanding that Satan is primarily an accuser helps the believer recognize these attacks for what they are: lies intended to separate them from the grace of God. Revelation asserts that this accuser has been "thrown down" — he has lost his power — which encourages the Christian to reject his accusations and to stand firm in the assurance that God does not condemn those who are in Christ.

sens: To establish someone in a place, to settle them as a colonist
To populate a place, to establish a colony there
To be installed, to remain in a place
G6052.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to install someone somewhere, to place them as one would plant a colony. It conveys the idea of founding and establishing durably: bringing a person to a place for them to settle there permanently.
2. Actively, the verb can also mean to populate, to colonize an entire area. It fills an empty space with inhabitants who will live there.
3. In the passive voice, the word means to be installed, to remain, to dwell oneself in a place. It is the state of one who is established somewhere. In James 4:5, the Spirit is described as the one whom God has made to "dwell" in us: God has placed Him in our hearts to remain there.
G6052.origine: The word comes from the root "katoik-", composed of "kata" (down, into) and "oikos" (house). It literally means to bring something into a house, that is, a home. This same root gives rise to "katoikia" (dwelling) and "katoikos" (inhabitant). The verb thus expresses the action of founding a home, establishing a dwelling.
G6052.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in James 4:5. In this verse, the apostle asserts that God has made the Spirit to "dwell" in us. The context concerns God's jealousy for those who follow Him: He has given us His Spirit to live in us, established in our hearts as in a home. The word emphasizes the divine initiative and the permanence of this presence. In ancient Greek texts, the verb often referred to the installation of colonists in a region or the establishment of populations in a city.
G6052.portee: This word reminds us that God does not give the Holy Spirit for a fleeting visit, but to dwell permanently. It is a dwelling, a home. This assures the believer that the Spirit does not leave those who trust in Christ: He establishes Himself there as in His house. This permanent presence transforms our understanding of the Christian life, not as an occasional help, but as a constant and intimate companionship.

sens: Lower, down
At a lower level
Of lesser value or importance
G6053.detail:
1. Below means "lower" in space, in contrast to what is above. It conveys the idea of something located under something else. Matthew 2:16 speaks of children "two years old and below," meaning children up to two years old inclusive, those who fall within the lower age category.
2. The word also expresses an inferior position in rank or value. What is "below" can designate something that occupies a secondary or lesser level in any order.
3. By extension, below can apply to any comparison: what is "below" a measure or limit does not reach it, it remains beneath.
G6053.origine: The word comes from the preposition "kata" (κατά), which means "down, towards the bottom." It is the comparative of an adverb indicating direction downwards. In ancient Greek, this same family of words is used to speak of anything that descends or is inferior. The adverb expresses movement or position from above to below, or simply a situation beneath a reference.
G6053.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 2:16, where Herod orders the killing of all the children of Bethlehem "two years old and below." In this context, it functions as a lower limit that includes all children up to that age, without exceeding it. It is a concrete and administrative usage: setting an age threshold below which victims are counted.
G6053.portee: This word reminds the reader of the precise cruelty of Herod's massacre. By setting an age limit, the narrative emphasizes that the king acted with calculation and method, not out of mere blind fury. This helps the believer understand that the child Jesus escaped a deliberate and total threat, which gives meaning to the divine protection of His birth.

sens: A low piece of furniture on which one lies down to sleep or rest
A stretcher or litter on which someone is transported lying down
G6055.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a little bed, a piece of furniture where one rests their body. It is a diminutive of the Greek word for "bed" (κλίνη), suggesting something more humble or modest than a large bed.
2. In the passage from Acts 5:15, it takes on the meaning of a stretcher or litter: the sick and infirm are "laid on beds and couches" in the streets, carried rather than lying down to sleep. It is a means of transporting them so that Peter's shadow might heal them.
G6055.origine: The word comes from the Greek κλίνη (klínē), which means "bed" or "couch." The diminutive suffix -άριον (-árion) indicates the smallness or humility of the object. A similar word, κλινίδιον (klinídion), also refers to a comparable form. The diminutive emphasizes that these beds on which the sick are laid are simple and small, likely portable cots or mats.
G6055.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 5:15. In this account, the apostles perform so many miracles in Jerusalem that crowds bring the sick "on beds and couches" to place them in the streets. The context shows a practical use: these little beds or stretchers serve to transport the infirm, exposing their need and facilitating their healing through divine intervention. It is a concrete detail that paints the scene of God's power in action at the heart of the early community.
G6055.portee: This verse illustrates how the nascent Church crowded around the apostles, convinced that God could heal the sick. It also shows the humility of the means employed: simple beds, not palaces — the Kingdom of God manifests among the poor and the weak, where faith rests.

sens: that which is hidden, concealed from view
that which is done away from public attention
that which is known only to God, invisible to man
G6058.detail: 1. The word literally designates what is hidden, removed from sight: Jesus speaks of the "secret place" where the Father sees what is done without a witness (Matthew 6:18). 2. By extension, it qualifies an action done without witnesses, away from public gaze: to fast in secret means to fast without anyone knowing. 3. The spiritual meaning is clearly evident in this passage: the Father sees in secret, meaning He knows what escapes human eyes and will reward it. What is secret to us is not secret to God.
G6058.origine: The Greek word κρυφαῖος comes from an Indo-European root expressing the idea of hiding or veiling. In classical Greek (in Pindar and Aeschylus), it simply meant "hidden, occult." In the New Testament, it carries the same idea of what escapes external sight, but the Christological teaching gives it a new depth: the secret of the heart before God.
G6058.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 6:18, in Jesus' teaching on almsgiving and fasting. Jesus emphasizes that disciples should not act for human glory, but in secret, knowing that the Father will see what is hidden from men and will reward it. This passage is at the heart of the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus redefines true piety: not an exhibition of virtue, but an inner authenticity recognized by God alone.
G6058.portee: This word teaches us a liberating truth: our acts of piety are only valuable if they are genuine before God, not before men. It calls us to reject complacency and the need for public recognition, and to cultivate a spiritual intimacy where the gaze of God is enough. This transforms our way of serving: less facade, more sincerity.

sens: To form a circle around something
To surround, encircle a position to block or attack it
G6059.detail: 1. The word describes the action of forming a circle or moving around something. This is the basic image: drawing a line that returns to its starting point while enclosing what is in the center. In Revelation 20:9, the enemy armies "invest" the camp of the saints — they deploy in a circle around it to take it. 2. The meaning sharpens to signify encircling a fortified position, a city, or a camp with the view of seizing or destroying it. It is a military term: to invest means to completely surround a place to prevent any escape and prepare for the assault.
G6059.origine: The word comes from the Greek κύκλος (kúklos), which means "circle." The verb κυκλεύω adds to this noun the idea of action: to make a circle, to move in a circle. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates the Hebrew סָבַב (sâbab), which means "to turn around" or "to surround." It is a very concrete family: the circle as form and as movement of protection or encirclement.
G6059.emploi: The word appears very rarely in the New Testament — a single certain occurrence in Revelation 20:9. It describes the moment when the armies of Gog and Magog, released after a thousand years, surround the camp of the saints and the beloved city (the New Jerusalem). The meaning is clearly military and apocalyptic: it is the final battle before the final judgment. The image of encirclement emphasizes the appearance of a total threat, even though it will be instantly broken by fire from heaven.
G6059.portee: This passage reminds Christians that even when the forces of evil seem to have completely surrounded the Church, the victory belongs to God alone. The investment of the camp of the saints is momentary and illusory: a single fire from heaven is enough to destroy them. It is an invitation to trust in the supreme and definitive power of the Lord.

sens: to transform one thing into another
to reverse the state or appearance of something
G6060.detail: 1. To transform one thing into another, by turning or flipping it into a new form. The starting image is one of movement that overturns or tips: one "turns around" a reality to convert it into its opposite. In James 4:9, the apostle calls believers to let their laughter "be turned into mourning" — this is the total inversion of a heart disposition, the transition from light joy to deep sorrow. 2. To reverse the state or appearance of something, to completely turn it over. This is less the idea of a simple modification than of a reversal: what was turned one way is turned the other. This nuance is clearly seen when James speaks of transforming joy into affliction — it is not softening joy, but completely overturning it.
G6060.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to turn around" or "to return" (meta- = around, trepō = to turn). This image of rotation or tipping is found in several words of the same family in ancient Greek. The verb expresses less a simple transformation than a complete reversal, a radical overturning of a disposition or state.
G6060.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in James 4:9. It is part of a call to repentance addressed to believers who seek the pleasures of the world: the apostle exhorts them to completely reverse their attitude, to make way for affliction and mourning instead of carefree joy. The context shows that this is not a simple superficial modification, but a deep conversion of the heart — a radical spiritual turnaround. Some ancient manuscripts offer a variant, but the meaning remains similar.
G6060.portee: This word from James challenges the believer regarding the seriousness of repentance. It teaches that turning to God does not consist of adding a little piety to a superficial life, but of radically reversing one's priorities and joys. For one who knows they have turned their back on God through sin, true change means allowing the sorrow of repentance to replace the false joy of the world — a transformation that comes from the heart and not from mere appearance.

sens: made of millstone, grinding stone
belonging to a mill or the grinding of grains
G6061.detail: 1. The word designates what is composed of a millstone — this large, round, heavy stone used to grind grain. In Revelation 18:21, an angel takes a stone "like a great millstone" to throw it into the sea: the image is that of a stone as massive and solid as a millstone, symbolizing definitive destruction. 2. More broadly, the adjective characterizes anything belonging to the mill or the work of grinding: a millstone, a grinding stone, the mechanism that crushes and transforms grain into flour. It is the world of the miller and daily grinding.
G6061.origine: The word comes from the Greek μύλος (mulos), which means "mill" or "millstone." The adjective μύλινος is regularly derived from this to express the idea of "belonging to the mill, made of millstone." It is a concrete word, stemming from the vocabulary of agricultural and artisanal work that every Mediterranean person knew well.
G6061.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:21. John uses it to evoke the fall of Babylon: an angel throws a huge stone "like a great millstone" into the sea. This choice of image is powerful: the millstone is heavy, it grinds, it crushes — it is the perfect symbol of irrevocable and total destruction. The city that had crushed the faithful under its weight will itself be crushed and will disappear forever.
G6061.portee: This image reminds us that the domination of evil, even when overwhelming and enduring, will not last. Just as a millstone is an instrument of grinding that reduces to nothing, divine justice will crush what opposes God. For the persecuted or tormented Christian by the power of evil around them, it is a promise of liberation and final justice.

sens: To have knowledge of something, to be informed
To know someone, to be in relationship with them
To understand, to perceive by the mind
To know how to do something, to have the ability
To recognize, to identify
To be aware, to realize
G6063.detail:
1. To have knowledge of something means to possess it in one's mind, to have learned or observed it. Matthew 6:8 illustrates this: the Father "knows" what you need — He possesses this knowledge even before you express it to Him. It is a complete and certain knowledge.

2. To know someone means to recognize them, to discern them, often through a prolonged or intimate relationship. In John 10:4, the sheep "know" the voice of the shepherd — they recognize it among all others and trust Him. It is a personal and living knowledge.
