3. To understand means to grasp the meaning or reality of something. Luke 9:47 states that Jesus "saw" the thoughts of their hearts — He discerned, He understood their hidden intentions.

4. To know how to do something means to master an action or possess a skill. It is to be able to accomplish something, as suggested in Mark 2:10 when Jesus asks what you "know" about the forgiveness of sins — understanding what He can do.

5. To recognize means to identify someone or something as real, as possessing a certain quality. Matthew 28:5 provides an example: "Do not be afraid... I know... that you are looking for Jesus" — to recognize Him, to identify Him with certainty.

6. To be aware, to realize means to become conscious of a moral or spiritual reality. Romans 2:2 asserts, "we know that the judgment of God... is according to truth" — an intimate certainty, an inner conviction.
G6063.origine: This Greek verb comes from an ancient Indo-European root related to vision and perception. The equivalent Hebrew word, "yada" (יָדַע), shares the same imagery: to know is to "see" in a profound sense, to have an intimate perception. The form "oida" found in Greek literally means "I have seen" (hence I know) — it is a perfect tense that expresses an established, lasting knowledge. The family includes words like "idea" (form, appearance) and "eidos" (aspect): to know is in some way to have "seen" and retained that vision.
G6063.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the New Testament (263 occurrences). It commonly denotes the knowledge that God has of all things — Matthew 6:8 emphasizes that the Father "knows" your needs. It also describes personal knowledge: the disciples and the sheep "know" Christ in a living way. In debates with the Pharisees, it expresses a certain but contested knowledge ("do you know...?"), often leading to a revelation or a refutation. In Paul, in 2 Corinthians 5:11, "knowing" the fear of the Lord becomes a conviction that transforms action. The verb also carries a personal assurance: "I know whom I have believed" (2 Timothy 1:12), where knowing becomes an unwavering certainty of trust.
G6063.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb reveals two fundamental truths. First, that God knows us — not from a distant knowledge, but an intimate and caring one: He "knows" what we need before we ask. Second, that the Christian faith rests on a living knowledge of Christ, not on an abstract dogma: we can "know Him" as the sheep know the voice of the shepherd. This knowledge is never purely intellectual; it engages trust, relationship, and life transformation.

sens: the group of servants in a household
domestic staff attached to a master
G6064.detail:
1. The word refers to the group of servants who work in a house under the authority of a master. It is a collective term: not an isolated servant, but all the domestic staff as a group. In Matthew 24:45, Jesus speaks of a servant appointed by his master "over his people" — that is, tasked with directing and feeding all the servants of the house.
2. By extension, the word can refer to the state or condition of domestic servitude, the set of tasks and duties that fall to those who live in service to a master, in daily dependence and obedience.
G6064.origine: The word comes from the root οἰκ- (house) and the suffix -ετεία which forms abstract nouns denoting a condition or function. It is built on οἰκέτης (house servant), which designates one who belongs to a house as a slave or domestic servant. The root οἰκ- is the same as in οἶκος (house) and expresses everything that belongs to the domestic universe, to the home.
G6064.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 24:45. Jesus uses it in the parable of the faithful servant: a master entrusts a servant with the responsibility to feed and direct his domesticity — the entire household under his authority. The context is about the duties of the servant towards those who depend on him, with the backdrop of the master's return. The word emphasizes the collective nature of this responsibility: it is not just about serving the master, but caring for the entire household that is under his authority.
G6064.portee: This parable, which features this word, speaks to the heart of the Christian: each of us may be called to a pastoral responsibility towards others, even in ordinary tasks. The word reminds us that in the Church, those who serve do not do so alone, but as members of a community; and those who lead must do so with faithfulness and prudence, spiritually nourishing those entrusted to them, in anticipation of giving an account to Jesus.

sens: one who constructs buildings
one who spiritually edifies
one who rejects or refuses
base or foundation of a work
G6065.detail: 1. The builder is primarily the worker or architect who constructs houses and buildings — one who lays stones and assembles materials. 2. In a figurative sense, it is one who spiritually edifies, who builds the Church: in Acts 4:11, Jesus, rejected by the builders of Israel, becomes the cornerstone, the foundation of all the spiritual edifice that God is building. 3. In contrast, the builders who reject the stone (Jesus) are those who refuse the foundation that God has chosen and thus risk collapsing.
G6065.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to build" (oikos = house) to which a suffix is added to denote one who performs the action. It is a simple and concrete term, borrowed from the common language of construction, which the Bible applies to the spiritual building of the Church and the rejection of Jesus by the Jewish authorities.
G6065.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 4:11, where Peter quotes Psalm 118 while addressing the Sanhedrin. The "builders" refer to the religious leaders of Israel who rejected Jesus — the priests, the elders, the scribes — who thought they could build the edifice of God's people without Him. This image contrasts the vanity of their human constructions with the divine plan.
G6065.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that Jesus is the true foundation, not only of the Church but of all spiritual life. It invites us to recognize who truly builds and not to build our lives on sand, but on Christ — the stone that the leaders of the people had rejected. It is a call to examine on what foundation we are building.

sens: Lack of trust in God and His power
Deficiency of faith that paralyzes action and courage
Doubt that prevents belief in divine promises
G6066.detail:
1. Unbelief is a lack of trust in God and what He can accomplish. It is not truly believing in His power, even when one claims to believe. At the moment when the disciples cannot heal a sick child, Jesus rebukes them for their unbelief — they do not trust in God's power to act through them (Matthew 17:20).

2. It is also a paralyzing doubt: instead of acting with assurance because one relies on God, one hesitates, fears, and remains powerless. Jesus explains that if the disciples had true confidence, even as small as a mustard seed, they could command a mountain to move — unbelief is the opposite of that confidence which dares to ask God and expects Him to respond.

3. It is an obstacle to the impossible: everything that seems unachievable becomes possible once one truly believes, but unbelief confines us to the "it's impossible". It tells us that God's promises are not true or will not apply to us.
G6066.origine: The word comes from two roots: oligos (small, few) and pistis (faith, trust). Unbelief is not the total absence of faith, but a very weak, narrow faith, incapable of soaring. It is a faith that does not dare to truly believe or hope. The word describes this intermediate state of the disciple who says he believes but whose trust is so thin that it cannot accomplish anything.
G6066.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 17:20, in a very significant context. The disciples have just failed to heal a child possessed by a demon. Jesus tells them that this failure comes from their unbelief — a trust too weak for God to act through them. It is a gentle but firm word of reproach: Jesus does not say that they have no faith at all, but that their trust is insufficient, too measured, too cautious. He urges them to take the step toward a true faith that surrenders to God's power.
G6066.portee: For today's Christian, this word highlights a reality: one can call oneself a believer and yet allow doubt to paralyze us. Unbelief is not always the outright refusal to believe, but the smallness of our trust, which prevents us from praying with assurance or expecting real answers from God. Jesus invites us to examine the strength of our own trust: do we really dare to believe in what God has promised, or is our faith still too thin?

sens: With difficulty, just
Almost not, with great effort
G6067.detail:
1. The word expresses something that is done or accomplished with difficulty, just barely exceeding a critical threshold. In 2 Peter 2:18, it describes people who "have barely escaped" those who live in deception — they have just managed to free themselves, but it was difficult, and this fragile progress makes them vulnerable to the seductions of false teachers.
2. By extension, it emphasizes weakness or insufficiency: what occurs "barely" is at the limit, fragile, not solid — here, a very recent and hesitant conversion.
G6067.origine: The word comes from the adjective ὀλίγος ("few, little, rare"), of which it is the adverb. The root refers to the idea of "few": little space, little strength, little time. The adverb in -ως in Greek expresses manner or circumstance. The meaning "barely" arises from this notion of "few" applied to an effort or a success: just enough, no more.
G6067.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:18. Peter denounces the false teachers who seduce unstable souls. These souls are described as "barely escaped" from the immorality of the wicked — the "barely" emphasizes that their liberation is recent, incomplete, and that they lack spiritual solidity, hence their propensity to fall back into new traps and desires.
G6067.portee: This word reveals the fragility of one who has just left sin: conversion is not a fortress, but a fragile new beginning. It warns us that hearts "barely" escaped from evil remain exposed to temptations and seductions, and that they particularly need solid Word and strengthening in the truth. It is a lesson in vigilance and compassion towards young converts.

sens: A fog or light mist
A veil that obscures vision or judgment
Figuratively, spiritual darkness and obscurantism
G6068.detail:
1. The word designates a light fog, a fine mist that floats in the air — less thick than a dense cloud, but enough to reduce visibility. It is a natural image drawn from the Mediterranean climate.
2. Figuratively, it describes a veil that covers the eyes or mind, preventing clear sight or understanding. In 2 Peter 2:17, false teachers are described as "clouds": empty promises that shimmer with something without delivering anything, like fog that hides the landscape.
3. By extension, the word symbolizes moral and spiritual darkness, lies, and deception. The "cloud" evokes what veils the truth and plunges into darkness.
G6068.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that expresses the idea of something that covers, that envelops. It appears in ancient Greek poets (Homer) to describe light mists and clouds. The Hebrew word from the Old Testament often translated this way is עָנָן (anân), which means both the natural cloud and the manifestation of divine presence. Here, the Greek gives a darker hue: an obscurity that misleads rather than a divine covering.
G6068.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:17. The apostle Peter uses it to describe false teachers: people who, like clouds without water carried by the wind, make empty promises. They seem to carry a load (promises of freedom, enlightenment), but give nothing. The image underscores the contrast between the seductive appearance and total emptiness, and it announces that these impostors are destined for eternal darkness. The context shows how this word is used to ridicule and condemn spiritual lies.
G6068.portee: This word helps the Christian reader to identify and be wary of false teachers: they never present themselves as deceivers, but as impressive and promising figures. The "cloud" reminds us not to be seduced by empty words or deceptive appearances. It also invites us to ask God to dissipate any fog — any lie — from our judgment, so that we may see clearly in the truth of the Gospel.

sens: In all places, throughout a territory or the world
G6069.detail: 1. This word literally means "in all places." It describes something that extends or operates over the entirety of a geographical space without exception. In Acts 21:28, Paul's accusers cry out that he "preaches everywhere," meaning that his preaching of the Gospel has spread to many regions and has touched many people; the adverb emphasizes the extraordinary scope of his influence.
G6069.origine: The Greek word πανταχῆ comes from the root παν- (pan-) meaning "all" and the suffix -ακῆ which marks place or direction. The same root pan- appears in words like "pandemonium" or "panorama" in modern French. It is a locative adverb that expresses the idea of spatial totality, very close to the French "partout."
G6069.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 21:28, during the uproar against Paul in Jerusalem. The crowd accuses him of preaching "everywhere" against the Jewish law and the temple, thus denouncing the universal scope of his apostolic ministry. The use of the word reinforces the accusation by showing that Paul is not acting locally but on a large scale, which makes the threat, in the eyes of his adversaries, even more serious.
G6069.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian message, even humble at its beginnings, possesses remarkable expansion power. It also highlights how the enemies of the Gospel already perceived its ability to spread everywhere, without limits or borders. For the reader, it is an invitation to see the power of the apostolic testimony and the vigor of the nascent Church.

sens: Set up a camp, establish militarily around a place
Surround, encircle from all sides
G6070.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of setting up a military camp, establishing troops around a strategic location. It is the image of an army pitching its tents, fortifications, and equipment to occupy a position. In Luke 19:43, Jesus announces that enemies will "establish a siege" around Jerusalem, threatening the city with siege.
2. By extension, the word means to completely encircle, surround in such a way as to cut off any escape. It conveys the idea of a military presence that encloses and isolates a place from all sides, threatening and inevitable.
G6070.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "para" (beside, next to) and "ballō" (throw, place). The primary image is that of placing something beside or among the lines of battle. In a military context, it has specialized to denote the establishment of a camp near an enemy position, hence the meaning of encirclement and siege. The root "ballō" (to throw) appears in many Greek words related to arrangement and placement.
G6070.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 19:43, in Jesus' prophecy concerning the destruction of Jerusalem. Jesus warns that enemies will "establish a siege" around the city, encircling it and bringing it to ruin. The context is one of divine judgment on Jerusalem for rejecting the messianic peace. The verb emphasizes the inevitability of the siege and the complete encirclement of the city.
G6070.portee: This word reminds the reader of the certainty of Jesus' words regarding judgment and the Resurrection. It shows that God will fulfill His warnings, and that unbelief in the Gospel leads to serious and irreversible consequences. It is an invitation to take seriously the call to repentance and faith.

sens: Further away, at a greater distance
Beyond a fixed limit
Beyond what is necessary, in excess
G6071.detail:
1. The word evokes the idea of exceeding a spatial or temporal limit: going further than expected, beyond a landmark. In Acts 19:39, it refers to questions that go "beyond" the discussed point, adding to what has preceded: "And if you have in mind other matters…"

2. It designates what crosses a boundary or threshold: not only this, but also that and many other things. It conveys the idea of surpassing what was initially considered or deemed sufficient.

3. In a metaphorical context, the word can express excess or surplus: going too far, asking for more than necessary, stepping outside acceptable limits.
G6071.origine: The word comes from the preposition πέρα (péra), which means "on the other side of, beyond." It is a comparative and adverbial form: it reinforces the idea of surpassing, crossing over. The root evokes movement that crosses a limit, going from one side to the other. Greek often uses this preposition to express both the limit and its surpassing.
G6071.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 19:39. It is used to refer to questions or matters (the issues the Ephesians want to resolve) that exceed the scope of the tumultuous assembly where Paul speaks. These "other matters" will be addressed in a legal, orderly assembly. The context shows that it is about exceeding the present framework: not only the immediate questions but also everything that goes beyond them, everything that goes further.
G6071.portee: This word reminds us that there are legitimate limits to discussions and actions: when a matter exceeds the context in which it is raised, when it goes beyond its limits, it is necessary to change context, authority, or method. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize when a situation or question is outside its jurisdiction and to seek resolution in the right place, with the appropriate authorities.

sens: Attach or fix something around an object
Ignite, produce fire
G6072.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the verb is to attach, to fix something around an object — for example, tying a rope, attaching a crown around the head. It is a compound verb: the prefix "peri" means "around," and the simple verb means "to touch" or "to fix."

2. In later usage of the Greek language, the verb takes on the meaning of igniting or lighting a fire. In Luke 22:55, after Jesus' arrest, the servants and guards "lit a fire in the midst of the courtyard" to warm themselves during the night — it is by this fire that Peter will approach to keep warm, just before denying his master.
G6072.origine: The verb comes from the Greek root "hapto" (to touch, to fix) preceded by the prefix "peri" (around). The basic image is therefore: "to touch around," "to fix around." The transition from the meaning "to fix around" to the meaning "to light a fire" is likely explained by the concrete act of surrounding wood or other materials around a flame to maintain it, and then by extension, to set fire to what surrounds the hearth.
G6072.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 22:55, where it describes the action of lighting a fire. The usage is concrete: in the context of the Passion, the fire that the high priest's servants light in the courtyard becomes the backdrop for the scene where Peter finds himself facing servants who recognize and question him. This detail is important for understanding the atmosphere of the scene: the fire, the warmth, the light — and Peter who draws near to the fire, physically close to the arrested Jesus but spiritually distancing himself.
G6072.portee: This word reminds us of a poignant image of the Passion: at the moment when Jesus is judged in the high priest's house, His disciples and He are separated. Peter, who swore to die with Him, warms himself by the fire lit by Jesus' enemies — a poignant image of cowardice, but also of human weakness in the face of fear. The detail of the fire highlights the contrast between carnal warmth and the coldness of faith that abandons.

sens: Absence of harshness or severity in character and speech
Benevolent and patient attitude towards others
Humility and moderation in behavior
G6073.detail:
1. Gentleness is primarily a quality of one who is not rude, angry, or aggressive: it is a certain softness of heart and speech. Imagine someone who speaks without shouting, who acts without brusqueness. It is the opposite of violence or outburst.
2. It also designates the attitude of one who treats others with kindness and patience, without overwhelming or harshly judging them. In 1 Timothy 6:11, the Apostle Paul asks Timothy, as a servant of God, to pursue this quality: to be gentle with those he encounters.
3. It finally encompasses a form of humility: the one who is gentle does not seek to dominate or impose their strength, but to serve with moderation. It is a virtue that tempers pride and harshness.
G6073.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and belongs to the same family as πραότης (praotès), which also means gentleness or meekness. These two words express one of the major values of Christian behavior: a controlled strength directed towards the good of others. The Greek root evokes the idea of something smoothed, softened, without roughness.
G6073.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:11. In this passage, Paul lists the virtues that the servant of God should seek: righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, and gentleness. It is therefore among the essential qualities of a mature and faithful Christian. Some ancient manuscripts have the word πραότης in its place, showing that these two terms are close in meaning and often interchangeable.
G6073.portee: For the Christian reader, this virtue reminds us that being a disciple does not mean being weak or without convictions, but possessing a gentle and benevolent strength. In a world of harshness and aggression, gentleness is a powerful testimony: it reflects the love of Christ and lends credibility to our message. It is a mark of spiritual maturity to seek this quality in daily life, especially in our relationships with others.

sens: The first founder of a family, the one from whom all other members descend
A distant patriarch, an ancestor from past generations
Figuratively, the spiritual father of a community, the one who originated it
G6074.detail:
1. The word designates the very first founder of a lineage, the father from whom the genealogy truly begins. He is the quintessential ancestor, the one who gave birth to the family. In Romans 4:1, Abraham is called our "father" (literally founding ancestor) according to the flesh: he is the one who begot the people of Israel.

2. More broadly, this word speaks of forebears, distant ancestors from whom we inherit blood and condition. It evokes the chain of generations that precede us.

3. In a more spiritual sense, it can designate one who established a tradition, a belief, a religious practice for all his descendants. Abraham is also the father of faith for believers.
G6074.origine: The Greek word comes from the combination of two elements: "pro-" (before, earlier) and "patēr" (father). Literally, it means "the father before," the one who was a father before us. It is related to the word "progonos" (ancestor) and reflects the idea that genealogy traces back to its origins. It is a common word among ancient Greek authors to speak of the founders of families or cities.
G6074.emploi: This word is infrequent in the New Testament: it appears only once in the Segond, in Romans 4:1. Paul uses it to speak of Abraham, the founding father of the Jewish people, to show that the question of justification rests upon him. The context is doctrinal: Paul examines what Abraham obtained through his works or through faith. Although the word is rare in New Testament Greek, it was a term widely used by historians and playwrights to honor ancestors.
G6074.portee: This word reminds Christians that our faith has roots, a history, founders. Abraham is not just a character from the past: he is our spiritual ancestor. This invites us to revisit the promises made to the one from whom we inherit, and to question what truly underpins our position before God — faith or the works of the law.

sens: A person who asks for alms to live
One who depends entirely on the charity of others
G6075.detail: 1. A beggar is a person reduced to asking for alms to subsist, typically standing by the roadside or in public places. In Mark 10:46, Bartimaeus, blind and poor, is sitting "by the roadside" as a beggar in Jericho: this is his daily condition. 2. The word also evokes a form of extreme destitution: the beggar depends entirely on the generosity of passersby and has no resources of his own. In John 9:8, the neighbors recognize the healed man by saying "the one who sat and begged," showing that his social identity was entirely linked to his begging.
G6075.origine: The word comes from the Greek "prosaitēs," composed of "pros" (toward) and "aiteō" (to ask). The image is of someone who goes "toward people" to "ask" them for something. It is a specific Greek word that precisely designates this social condition of the alms seeker, with no direct equivalent in Hebrew from the Old Testament, as the urban context and Greek social structures made this phenomenon particularly visible.
G6075.emploi: The word "beggar" appears only twice in the New Testament, always in Mark and John. In both cases, it refers to men in a state of great precariousness: Bartimaeus, who is both blind and a beggar in Jericho (Mark 10:46), and the man born blind in John 9, who before his healing was known by his neighbors as someone who "begged." These two healing accounts emphasize that Jesus also addresses the most visible and abandoned outcasts of society, those who survive by begging.
G6075.portee: These two encounters with beggars reveal Jesus' tenderness toward the most marginalized. Bartimaeus and the blind man from Jerusalem are not ignored but healed and restored: Jesus sees the one whom society no longer sees. For the Christian reader, the word "beggar" is a reminder that the Gospel primarily addresses the needy and that Jesus honors those whom the world rejects.

sens: To side with someone, to give them support
To lean toward, to be attracted to a person or cause
G6076.detail:
1. To cling to someone means to side with them, to give them support and to follow them. In Acts 5:36, we see how about four hundred men "rallied" to Theudas (literally: clung to him) to follow him as leader; but when Theudas was killed, all who had followed him were dispersed. The image is one of leaning, like a scale tipping to one side: people lean toward this one rather than that one.
2. Figuratively, the word can also express an inner inclination: to lean toward someone or something, to be attracted to a person, a doctrine, a cause. It is the movement of the heart or will that turns toward an object.
G6076.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: προσ- (toward) and κλίνω (to lean, incline). The basic image is that of a physical inclination, like when one tilts an object toward something. It has naturally extended to moral and social senses: to incline one's heart or allegiance toward someone.
G6076.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 5:36, where it describes the attitude of the four hundred men who clung to Theudas. The context is that of messianic or insurrectionary movements in Judea: men are attracted to a charismatic leader and align themselves with him. The passive used here ("to whom they rallied") shows an active willingness to cling, to submit to his authority.
G6076.portee: This word reminds us that adherence to a cause or a person engages the will and requires fidelity. In the context of the passage, it illustrates how the disciples of Theudas were dispersed after his death: clinging to a human leader, even sincerely, is vain if he is taken away. This implicitly contrasts with the attachment to Christ, who alone deserves such allegiance.

sens: father of Sopater of Berea
G6077.detail: Pyrrhus is mentioned only once in the New Testament as the father of Sopater, a disciple from Berea who accompanied the apostle Paul on his journey to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). His name literally means "red" or "fiery color" in Greek, but we know nothing else about him.
G6077.origine: The Greek name Pyrrhus (Πύρρος) comes from the adjective purrhós (πυρρός), which means "red" or "fiery color." It was a common name in the Greco-Roman world. Here, it simply designates the father of the disciple Sopater.
G6077.emploi: Pyrrhus appears only once in Scripture, in Acts 20:4, where he is identified as the father of Sopater of Berea. Sopater is part of the delegation that accompanied Paul on his last journey to Jerusalem, likely to bring the collections from the churches. The context shows that Pyrrhus was a member of a Christian family from Berea, an important city in Macedonia.

sens: first of all
at the beginning
initially
G6078.detail:
1. First of all, before anything else: the word indicates primacy or absolute precedence. It refers to what happens before or above everything. In Acts 11:26, the disciples are called "Christians" in Antioch "for the first time": this is the first occurrence, the first moment this name was given.
2. At the beginning, at the start of a process or story: the word situates an event at the starting point. It marks the temporal origin of a new reality that is established.
G6078.origine: The adverb comes from the adjective "prôtos" (πρῶτος) which means "first" in Greek. It is a very ancient word in the Greek language and very common for designating anything that is first in order, time, or importance. The adverbial form reinforces the idea of primacy or originality by marking the moment or instant of "for the first time."
G6078.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 11:26, where it highlights the foundational event of the name "Christians." Although the manuscript is unique, this usage is strategic: it marks not only a historical primacy (never before this moment had the disciples borne this name), but also an important ecclesial novelty. The context is that of the mission in Antioch, where non-Jews and Jews gathered together in the Church for the first time in a regular and visible manner.
G6078.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the name "Christian" was born from a new reality and a rupture: that of the merging of Jewish and Gentile communities around Jesus. It marks a historical and identity turning point in the early Church. Understanding this "for the first time" helps to see that Christianity does not emerge from nothing, but from the living and shared testimony around the name of the Lord.

sens: grain of wheat, cultivated cereal
food, provisions intended for consumption
staple foods of a person or community
G6079.detail:
1. The word σιτίον primarily refers to wheat and other cereals, this seed that is cultivated in fields and constitutes the fundamental food of ancient civilizations. It is the grain transformed into bread or flour. In Acts 7:12, when Jacob learns that there is wheat in Egypt, it refers to this harvest capable of feeding his family during the famine.
2. More broadly, the word encompasses all food supplies intended to sustain a person or a group. It conveys the idea of everything that is set aside for eating, which lasts for a certain time: a supply for three days, as they say in Greek, or the provisions one takes on a journey.
3. Wheat also symbolically represents sustenance, life itself: to have wheat is to have the means to live. In the context of Acts 7, it concerns survival in the face of famine.
G6079.origine: The word σιτίον comes from an ancient Greek root related to nourishment. In Greek, the word is closely associated with the concept of solid food, as opposed to drinks. Wheat was in the Mediterranean antiquity what we today call "a strategic commodity": essential for survival, an object of trade and sometimes conflict. The word reflects the vital importance of this cereal in the economy and daily life of the ancient Greeks and the peoples of the Bible.
G6079.emploi: The word σιτίον is used only once in the Segond in the sense of wheat in Acts 7:12, in Stephen's speech recounting the story of Jacob and the famine. However, in the classical Greek literature that transmits it, it regularly designates provisions, food, all the items intended for consumption, particularly in a context of travel or collective sustenance (such as for soldiers or citizens supported by the state). The meaning shifts from the concrete (the cereal itself) to the general (everything one eats to survive).
G6079.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not speak in abstractions: it evokes famine, hunger, the vital need for food, and God's providence which, through Joseph, brings wheat to Egypt to save a family, then a people. It invites us to see that God provides for essential needs and that material provisions are part of His benevolent plan. It is also an invitation to gratitude for what we have: the daily bread, which we ask for in the Lord's Prayer, begins with the reality of wheat and the work that produces it.

sens: woman of the family, related by blood or marriage
G6080.detail: 1. The word designates a woman who belongs to the family, either by blood or by marriage. It is a female relative, a consanguineous. In Luke 1:36, the angel Gabriel tells Mary that her "relative" Elizabeth, although old and previously barren, has conceived a son — she is likely a cousin or a more distant relative of Mary.
G6080.origine: The Greek word comes from *sungenes* ("of the same origin"), formed from *syn* ("with, together") and *genos* ("family, race, origin"). It is the feminine form of an adjective that designates someone from the same clan or household. In Hebrew, words like *qa­rov* (close) or *mishpaha* (family) express a similar idea.
G6080.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 1:36. Luke uses it to establish a familial link between Elizabeth and Mary, which reinforces the miraculous nature of the account: two women from the same family, one young (Mary), the other old and barren (Elizabeth), each receiving the announcement of a miraculous pregnancy — that of Elizabeth due to her advanced age, that of Mary due to her virginity.
G6080.portee: This word reminds the reader that God's promises were fulfilled within a real family, with ties of flesh and blood. The link between Elizabeth and Mary also highlights a spiritual continuity: the Mother of the Messiah and the mother of the Forerunner are united not only by blood but by their obedience to God and their role in His plan of salvation.

sens: to collapse, to crumble
to occur suddenly, to happen
to be in agreement, to correspond exactly
G6081.detail:
1. To fall or to collapse: the word depicts the collapse of a structure. In Luke 6:49, the house "fell" when the torrent struck it — not just a simple tipping over, but a catastrophic collapse, a complete ruin, because it had no solid foundation.
2. To occur, to happen: in a figurative sense, the word describes an event that happens, falls upon someone — an accident, an illness, a stroke of fate — like something that suddenly descends.
3. To be in agreement, to correspond, to coincide: the word can also express an exact concordance, two things that "fall together" at the same point, which fit perfectly with one another.
G6081.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb πίπτω (piptō, "to fall") with the prefix συν (syn, "together"). The image is that of several things falling together, converging in the same fall or event. It is a compound verb that ancient Greek authors used to express both physical collapse and coincidences or misfortunes that "fall" upon someone at the same time.
G6081.emploi: The word appears only once in the preserved New Testament, in Luke 6:49. Jesus uses it in the parable of two houses: the one that collapses because it lacks a foundation. In non-biblical Greek texts (Homer, Herodotus, Thucydides), this verb is much more frequent and carries several nuances: battles that meet, events that occur, circumstances that coincide. Here, in the Gospel, Jesus chose this verb to emphasize not only the material collapse but also the totality and suddenness of the disaster.
G6081.portee: This word from Jesus invites the believer to carefully examine the foundation of their spiritual life. A house built on the rock will stand firm; a house without a foundation can only collapse. It is a call to build one's faith on Christ and His Word, not on unstable principles. The word "fall" emphasizes the complete collapse: not a repairable crack, but a ruin.

sens: to share knowledge of something, to be complicit or a witness
to be self-aware, to know oneself
to have a particular conscience, especially a sense of guilt
G6083.detail:
1. The verb σύνοιδα combines two ideas: to be with (σύν) and to know (οἶδα). In its primary sense, it means to share knowledge with others, to be informed or complicit. It is to know a secret in the company of another, as in Acts 5:2, where Ananias and Sapphira act together in their deception.
2. The verb can also refer to self-awareness: to be aware of one's own thoughts, feelings, or actions. It is a form of internal knowledge, a lucidity about what is happening within us.
3. Very often in ancient and biblical Greek usage, this word expresses moral consciousness, particularly guilt or innocence regarding one's own actions. In 1 Corinthians 4:4, Paul declares, "I am not aware of anything against myself," meaning he is not conscious of wrongdoing within himself: he has no accusations to make against his own conscience, no personal reproaches that gnaw at him.
G6083.origine: The word is composed of the prefix σύν (with) and the verb οἶδα (to know), which is a perfect tense with present meaning in ancient Greek. This composition suggests shared knowledge or an inward-facing conscience. The root goes back to Indo-European and connects with French words like "voir" and "vision." In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this word often translates יָדַע (yadà), the Hebrew verb "to know" in a broad sense.
G6083.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament according to the provided data: in 1 Corinthians 4:4, where Paul uses it to express his personal innocence before God. He says, "I am not aware of anything against myself," literally "nothing has consciousness against me." This is a statement of integrity: the apostle has no hidden malice, no secret guilt that contradicts his ministry. The word, although rare in the New Testament, was known and used in the Septuagint and classical Greek literature to express both complicity (being aware of an action) and inner moral consciousness.
G6083.portee: This word helps the Christian understand that there is an internal conscience, an intimate knowledge of one's own intentions and heart. Paul uses it to remind us that our responsibility before God does not depend solely on the judgment of others, but also on the purity of our own conscience. It is a call to honesty towards oneself and towards God: a life of faith requires a clear conscience, not gnawed by hidden guilt. For the modern reader, this word invites sincere self-examination in prayer.

sens: man from Corinth, friend of Paul
G6084.detail: 1. Titius Justus is a resident of Corinth who welcomes Paul during his stay in the city. This man, bearing the Latin nickname "Justus" (just), offers hospitality to the apostle when the synagogue rejects him. It is in his house that Paul establishes his preaching place and where the Christian community of Corinth forms (Acts 18:7).
G6084.origine: The name Τίτιος (Titios) is a Latin name transcribed into Greek, common in the Roman world of the time. The nickname "Justus" literally means "just" in Latin and was held by several Roman figures. This double name reflects the Greco-Roman context of Corinth, where Latin names were frequent.
G6084.emploi: Titius Justus appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:7. At this point in the narrative, Paul has just been rejected by the synagogue of Corinth and needs a place to continue his ministry. Titius Justus, a God-fearing worshiper sympathetic to Judaism, offers his home. His intervention is crucial: it allows the continuation of Paul's missionary work in the city and marks a turning point where the Church separates from the synagogue.
G6084.portee: Titius Justus embodies the believer who stands alongside God's servants in difficult times. His generous welcome shows how Christian hospitality becomes the concrete foundation of the emerging Church's life, replacing closed religious structures. His example encourages the reader to recognize that God often uses simple and welcoming people to accomplish His work.

sens: narrow opening made in something
eye of a sewing needle
figuratively: nearly insurmountable obstacle
G6085.detail: 1. The word designates a perforation, an opening that goes through a material. In Luke 18:25, it refers to the eye of the needle, that tiny orifice through which the thread passes: it is an opening so small that it strikingly contrasts with the enormous size of a camel. 2. This is the image Jesus uses to express extreme difficulty: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. The hole thus becomes the very figure of the impossible or the nearly impossible.
G6085.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to pierce" or "to hole." It is a concrete term, borrowed from everyday vocabulary: one who sews is well acquainted with the hole of their needle. The word has no special connotation; it is simply the opening made in an object.
G6085.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 18:25, in the mouth of Jesus. Jesus teaches that entry into the kingdom of God is impossible for one who places their trust in riches: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. This striking image underscores the radical incompatibility between attachment to earthly goods and access to eternal life with God.
G6085.portee: This image of the eye of the needle invites us to examine where our trust lies. Jesus does not say that entry into the kingdom is impossible for the rich in itself, but that one who places their security in riches shuts the door. The absurd contrast (a camel in the eye of a needle) helps us grasp how urgent it is to detach our hearts from material goods to give them to the Lord.

sens: small ear, outer ear
cut or injured ear
G6090.detail:
1. The word designates the small external ear, the pavilion visible on the side of the head. It is a diminutive term of the common word for "ear," which emphasizes its distinct and recognizable character. In Mark 14:47 and John 18:10, during Jesus' arrest, it is precisely this visible and vulnerable ear that a disciple cuts off from the servant of the high priest.
2. By extension, the word refers to the ear in its state of injury or mutilation — that which has been cut, torn, or damaged. The two biblical uses report this same violent act: Peter cuts off the right ear of Malchus (John 18:10), an incident that Luke also reports, but which Mark and John designate with this specific word.
G6090.origine: The word comes from a Greek root related to hearing and perception. It is a diminutive of ôtion ("ear"), formed with the suffix -arion which gives a nuance of smallness or particularity. This form emphasizes the ear as a precise and identifiable part of the body, rather than the auditory organ in its general function.
G6090.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two parallel accounts of Jesus' arrest: Mark 14:47 and John 18:10. In both cases, it designates the severed ear of the servant of the high priest — named Malchus in John — at the moment when the disciples attempt to resist militarily to the arrest. It is a concrete and dramatic detail of the passion, reported without judgment but which strongly contrasts with the attitude of forgiveness and non-violence that Jesus later demonstrates.
G6090.portee: This account of the severed ear challenges the Christian regarding the temptation to defend Jesus through force and carnal combat. Peter's act shows impulsiveness and misunderstanding of God's plan; Jesus' reaction (reported in Luke 22:51) which heals this wound teaches mercy and victory through accepted suffering rather than through violence.

sens: to leave a place by going away
to abandon, to leave definitively
G6092.detail:
1. To go out means to leave a place, to cross its threshold to go elsewhere. This is the most concrete and simplest meaning: one goes out of a house, a city, a country. In Hebrews 11:15, Abraham and his family "went out" of their homeland (Chaldea) — they left the place where they were born to follow God's call.
2. The verb can also evoke the idea of abandoning, of leaving definitively: not a quick visit, but a departure that breaks with the past. In the same verse, it speaks of those who "had in mind the place from which they had gone out" — that is, the country they had left and to which they could have returned. Here, "to go out" emphasizes the break: they turned their backs on their former life.
G6092.origine: The Greek word ἐκβαίνω is formed from ἐκ (ek, "out of") and βαίνω (bainō, "to walk, to go"). It literally means "to walk out of," "to go outside." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this same concept is often rendered by עָלָה (alah), which primarily means "to go up" but also refers to departure, especially in the expression "to go up and leave a place." The Greek verb captures the idea of physical movement and rupture.
G6092.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:15. It is used to describe the departure of the patriarchs — Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob — who left their homeland. The author of the epistle reminds us that these men of faith broke with their past and never returned to the land from which they came: it is not a simple journey, but an exodus, an act of trust in God's promise. The context of Hebrews 11 (the chapter of faith) gives the verb a spiritual tone: to go out becomes the visible sign of an inner faith that accepts losing everything to follow God.
G6092.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that faith in God sometimes requires leaving our landmarks, our earthly securities — our "homelands" — to walk toward what God promises. Abraham and the patriarchs teach us that true wealth is not in returning to the known, but in faithfulness to the one who calls us. "To go out" is therefore not an act of fleeing, but of joyful obedience.

sens: to speak proudly of oneself or what one possesses
to exaggerate the importance of something
to claim an unearned glory
G6094.detail:
1. To boast means to speak with pride about one's merits, qualities, or possessions — it is to praise oneself before others. In James 3:5, the tongue "boasts of great things": it claims greatness, a power that it proudly asserts, as if it dominated everything.
2. The verb can also refer to the act of exaggerating the importance of a reality: the tongue boasts (it claims greatness) while being a "small member" (James 3:5). It is to claim more than one deserves.
3. To boast is finally to attribute to oneself a glory, a dignity that one does not truly possess — it is a failure of humility and recognition of the truth about oneself.
G6094.origine: The Greek word αὐχέω comes from the root αὔχη, which literally means "boastful speech" or "boasting." It is a word from the family of language and assertion: to speak with exaggeration about oneself. The starting image is that of a voice that rises to proclaim its own glory.
G6094.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in James 3:5. It describes the tongue that "boasts of great things": in this context of warning against the destructive effects of speech, James uses this verb to show the pride and pretension that often accompany human speech. The tongue is presented as an organ that claims an exaggerated importance, while it is tiny and can cause enormous damage — like a small fire that ignites a great forest.
G6094.portee: This word challenges us about our words and our relationship to ourselves. It invites us to recognize how the tongue can be the seat of pride and boasting. By showing us that even a "small" thing like the tongue can be dominated by pretension, Scripture calls us to vigilance and humility in our words, and to let the Spirit purify our speech.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus from the tribe of Judah, father of Amminadab
G6095.detail: 1. Arni is a man from the tribe of Judah who lived during the time of the united Israelite monarchy. He appears in the genealogy that Luke lists to show the descent of Jesus from Judah (Luke 3:33), where he is called Admin in some translations, but the original Greek text bears the name Arni. He is the father of Amminadab and the son of Hezron, placing him among the direct ancestors of Christ according to the lineage of Judah.
G6095.origine: The name Arni (Greek form of the Hebrew name) designates a historical figure from the Old Testament. This name appears in the genealogy of Ruth (Ruth 4:19), where he is mentioned as the son of Hezron. The New Testament takes up this same genealogy in Greek, placing Arni in the continuity of the transmission of the messianic promise through the lineage of Judah.
G6095.emploi: Arni is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:33, in the genealogy of Jesus. His name appears among the ancestors of Christ listed by the Evangelist Luke, who traces the lineage from Jesus back to Adam through Judah. This genealogy establishes that Jesus descends from the tribe of Judah and inherits the promise made to David regarding an eternal king from his lineage.
G6095.portee: Arni represents a link in the unbroken chain of ancestors that connects Jesus to Judah and Abraham. The mention of his name in the genealogy shows that God has consistently guided the history of Israel toward the fulfillment of his messianic promise, and that Jesus is not an accident of history but the culmination of a divine plan prepared long ago.
